title: 虚假移动游戏广告：英国监管机构加强监测，美国机构保持不介入
content:
Fake mobile game ads: UK regulator steps up monitoring while US agencies stay hands-off – Mobilegamer.biz
Skip to content
The UK’s Advertising Standards Authority has told us that mobile game advertisers who keep running misleading ads could be referred to Trading Standards, while regulators in the US remain largely non-interventionist.
The ASA recently
banned ads from King, Scopely, Dark War Survival publisher Omnilojo and Vistrex
for showing gameplay that didn’t reflect the actual games.
The authority has since told us that repeatedly running a banned ad, or one very similar to it, “could lead to the expansion of sanctions and the exploration for further account-level action from the platforms.”
It added: “The ultimate sanction would be a referral to Trading Standards under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (DMCCA).”
The four rulings didn’t stem from complaints; the ASA said it had been aware of fake mobile game ads for a while and that, despite several rulings over the years, the issue persists.
It identified the recent Farm Heroes Saga, Pixel Flow and Dark War Survival cases “through proactive monitoring to provide wider-reaching precedent”. To do this, the ASA uses its Active Ad Monitoring system, which can scrape public ad libraries.
The watchdog said it has received complaints about the issue “fairly consistently over the years”, and has seen “outcry from frustrated gamers online that nothing seems to be being done about this.”
The ASA said the practice is also unfair to advertisers who don’t want to mislead consumers, and who “see the reputational damage of this practice on both the mobile gaming sector and the digital advertising ecosystem.”
“Consumers shouldn’t be tricked into downloading a game, and possibly spending hours playing it, only to find it is nothing like the ads,” said the ASA. “We want to work to level the playing field so that reputable advertisers do not feel disadvantaged competing against hyper-optimised ads whose focus is driving downloads at the expense of misleading consumers.”
It’s a different story in the US, where the Federal Trade Commission says it takes “each situation on a case-by-case basis”. It said it defines an advertisement as deceptive “if it is likely to mislead consumers acting reasonably in the circumstances and is material to consumers”.
The FTC said it doesn’t track complaints about this kind of advertising as a separate category, but pointed to its
case against Genshin Impact maker Cognosphere
, over allegations that it misled players about the odds of winning prizes, as the closest it has come.
It added that it has jurisdiction over foreign advertisers “if their actions affect US consumers.”
The National Advertising Division, the US self-regulatory body, said it routinely monitors the mobile games space, but has not seen a large number of cases involving mobile games. Its two main cases, against Play Perfect’s Solitaire Smash and Mobile Fox’s Solitaire Arena in 2024, focused on earnings claims. “Advertisers must not overpromise and underdeliver,” said NAD VP Phyllis Marcus.
“In those cases, we did not examine demonstrations of game play,” she said. Advertisers who don’t take part in or follow the NAD’s recommendations can be referred to the FTC, state attorneys general and the platforms the ads ran on.
The NAD said an advertiser being based outside the US doesn’t affect its jurisdiction, but “could, however, affect the advertiser’s voluntar[y] compliance with our process.”
